title: Chu Berry and Roy Eldridge
summary: Budd recalls meeting Chu Berry in Chicago, describes his Hawkins-derived style, and Roy Eldridge's love of Hawkins and Armstrong records.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Now there's another man, Chu Berry.
Oh, Chu Berry, now he was a guy --
Tenor sax@phone.
This guy was phenomenal. The first
time I ever met Chu Berry he came to Chicago with Fletcher Henderson, and him and Roy Eldridge was boon coons -- they was runnin' around and we -- we used to go --
(Simultaneous remarks)

-- around and jam all the time. Sometimes Art Tatum would come in town, and we'd -- Teddy Wilson and Keg Gag, my brother, Mel Hinton, all of us, we'd go out to all of the after hour joints and whatnot and blow. And Chu Berry was blowing so much horn, man.
Explain his style of playing, Budd.

Oh, this is -- how can I do this? I mean I've heard this man play. In fact, he made a record. He made a record with Lester Young. I think they were playing 'Lady Be Good.' Right? And he played -- he had his own thing, plus you could see the Hawk influence. Yet, you know, it's just like anything else. If you copy somebody, like whichever -- I think everybody has to do in life -- they must be inspired by someone, then finally you start to come into your own, and you start to be able to play yourself. But yet that tone quality was there, but then it went into his own. And he could play -- well, he had an individual style all of his own. Yet I know he must have been influenced by Hawk. It's very difficult for me to say --
Right.
He was fast. He knew all of the

changes. And he was most happy when he was playing. I mean this cat would really get into it, and if you wasn't careful, he would wash you away because he knew what he was doing on the horn. His spangles was just -- would fall into the right place.
Would you agree with me if I said his style -- like Coleman Hawkins was a -- being a pianist -- he early became -- he played all of his changes. But Chu was a rough man.
Oh, I see what you mean.
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- his style now. He would really --
(Simultaneous remarks)
Doo-doodle-doodle-doodle-doodle-doodle-doo, doo, doo, doo, doo-doodle-doodle, doo, doo, doo, y-u-u-h, y-u-u-h, yeah, I see what you mean by style now.
He really was like --
Oh, they hung all out like --
(Simultaneous remarks)

You know Roy Eldridge, when we used to run around together, and he would play, he had every record Coleman Hawkins made. And he had all of Pops's records. And between the two of them, I think is when he grew, because he could play all the Hawk solos on the trumpet, he could play all the Lewis solos on the trumpet, and I mean -- of course,
you could see that, ladies and gentlemen, in later years, when he and Hawk got together and started to making all of these records and working together and how so well they fit like a glove.
They made so many records for Commodore records.
Oh, man, they've made millions of records.
